summary: Defines a set of SNMP management objects for monitoring directory servers, so operators can watch how a directory service is behaving. It replaced RFC 1567.

plainLanguage.summary: A dashboard with gauges for a big address book server, so the people looking after it can see if it is busy or healthy.

subtitle: SNMP objects that let operators watch directory servers: entry counts, cache hits, operations, errors and peer contacts.

tldr.problem: Directory services (X.500, LDAP and similar) need to be monitored like any other network service, but RFC 1567 covered only X.500 directory system agents.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the SMIv2 module DIRECTORY-SERVER-MIB with three read-only tables: dsTable for per-server summaries, dsApplIfOpsTable for per-protocol operation counters and dsIntTable for interactions with peer servers.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 1567 and is incompatible with it. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 2605 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 1567.

sections.title: Purpose and the SNMP Framework
sections.content:
RFC 2605 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for monitoring directory servers. It obsoletes RFC 1567, the "X.500 Directory Monitoring MIB", and widens that specification to cover one or more directory servers, each of which may support several access protocols. The MIB is meant to be used together with the NETWORK-SERVICES-MIB.

The first section recaps the SNMP Network Management Framework: an architecture (RFC 2571), the Structure of Management Information (SMIv1 and SMIv2), the SNMP message protocols (SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3), the protocol operations, and a set of applications plus view-based access control. The module is written in SMIv2. A SMIv1 version can be produced by translation and must be semantically equivalent, except where objects are omitted because no translation is possible, such as those using Counter64.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a rulebook for a set of gauges on a directory server. Any manager that speaks the standard network-monitoring language can read them.

sections.title: The Directory Services Model
sections.content:
The memo's model is a set of Directory Servers that give clients, called Directory User Agents (DUA), access to a directory that may be local or distributed. A server may be an X.500 Directory System Agent running over the OSI suite, a (C)LDAP front end to one, a native LDAP server running directly over TCP or other protocols, a database acting as a backend, or any combination. A server has one or more application protocol interfaces, and uses them to talk to DUAs and to peer servers.

The directory holds entries, each a collection of attributes identified by a Distinguished Name (DN) and arranged in the Directory Information Tree. To answer a request a server can use its local database, chain the request to other servers, or return a referral. Its local database holds entries it masters, slave copies it keeps, and cached information gathered while running.

In connection-oriented mode a DUA binds to a server, which may authenticate it; in connectionless mode, as in CLDAP, there is no bind. The operations listed are Read, Compare, AddEntry, ModifyEntry, ModifyRDN, RemoveEntry, List, Search and Abandon, and some servers do not support all of them. CLDAP, for example, supports none of the update operations. Replicated data moves from a supplier server to a consumer server under a replication agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: A directory is a giant phone book kept by several helpers. Some helpers own the original pages, some keep copies, and some only remember answers they have heard before.

sections.title: MIB Model and Design
sections.content:
A directory manager should be able to watch every server in their domain, even when several run on one host. Three kinds of information matter: process resource use, network service details such as inbound and outbound associations and operational status, and information specific to the directory application. This MIB covers only the last; the others live in the NETWORK-SERVICES-MIB and the host-resources MIB. A group of servers is chosen by the administrator, and each one gets an entry in the matching NETWORK-SERVICES-MIB.

The design principle is stated as keeping the MIB as simple as possible. Its objects are divided into three tables: dsTable, dsApplIfOpsTable and dsIntTable. Static information about a server is not stored in the MIB. Instead, objects hold the Distinguished Name of the thing they refer to, so that management applications can look up details in the directory itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of copying everything into the gauges, the MIB keeps its design simple and points to the phone book itself for the details.

sections.title: The Three Tables
sections.content:
dsTable has one row per directory server. dsServerType is a BITS value saying whether the server is a front end (bit 0), a back end (bit 1) or both. dsServerDescription is a text description. Three gauges count entries: dsMasterEntries (mastered here), dsCopyEntries (systematic slave copies) and dsCacheEntries (non-systematic cached copies). Two counters, dsCacheHits and dsSlaveHits, count operations answered from the cache or from slave copies.

dsApplIfOpsTable has one row per application protocol interface. dsApplIfProtocol is an object identifier naming the protocol in use. Counters cover bind requests by kind (dsApplIfUnauthBinds, dsApplIfSimpleAuthBinds, dsApplIfStrongAuthBinds) and bind rejections (dsApplIfBindSecurityErrors). Further counters cover total requests in (dsApplIfInOps), each operation type (read, compare, addEntry, removeEntry, modifyEntry, modifyRDN, list, search), one-level and whole-subtree searches, referrals returned, operations chained to other servers, security errors, other errors, replication updates in and out, and bytes in and out.

dsIntTable records how this server interacts with peer servers. Each row has the peer's Distinguished Name and URL, plus sysUpTime timestamps for when the row was created, when the last attempt was made and when the last attempt succeeded. It also holds failures since the last success and cumulative failure and success counts. Rows are indexed by applIndex, dsApplIfProtocolIndex and dsIntEntIndex together.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three score sheets: one for each server's totals, one for each way people can talk to it, and one for how well it gets along with its neighbours.

sections.title: Groups and Compliance
sections.content:
The module is organised into three object groups. dsEntryGroup holds the dsTable objects. dsOpsGroup holds the dsApplIfOpsTable objects. dsIntGroup holds the peer-interaction objects.

Four compliance statements combine them. All require dsEntryGroup. The first needs nothing more. dsOpsCompliance adds dsOpsGroup, dsIntCompliance adds dsIntGroup, and dsOpsIntCompliance requires all three groups. An implementer can therefore choose how much of the MIB to support.
sections.plainLanguage: You do not have to build every gauge. The memo lets you pick a basic, a medium or a full set.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No object in this MIB has a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create. If the MIB is implemented correctly, an intruder cannot alter or create its objects through SNMP SET operations.

The values themselves can still be sensitive. They may reveal part of the directory system's configuration, which can passively increase its vulnerability, and could be used to analyse network usage and traffic patterns. The memo says it may be important in some environments to control read access and even to encrypt values sent over the network. Not all versions of SNMP offer a secure environment.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody can change the gauges, but peeking at them could still tell a snoop how your server works, so you may want to limit who can look.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1567
sections.content:
The one change the memo lists is a more general directory model in which several directory protocols coexist. The result is a generic Directory Server Monitoring MIB rather than an X.500-only one.

The module's revision notes say the new version is incompatible with the original, so the module was renamed from dsaMIB to dsMIB. It is registered as { mib-2 66 }. The original version, dated 25 November 1993, was published in RFC 1567.
sections.plainLanguage: The old gauges only worked for one kind of address book. The new set works for many kinds, so it got a new name.
